title: Accessible deep-body molecular imaging

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a broadly deployable imaging system that maps clinically useful molecular targets and biological processes deep inside the human body. It would combine sufficient target discrimination, depth, spatial resolution and imaging speed with acceptable safety and deployment cost. The goal is to make useful molecular measurements practical across more care settings; portability is one possible route to access, rather than a requirement that every system be handheld. This is a proposed capability, not an achieved integrated system.

Photoacoustic computed tomography, or PACT, is one enabling approach. It combines optical excitation with acoustic detection: light absorption supplies contrast, while detection of the resulting acoustic signals enables imaging beyond the optical diffusion limit. This joins aspects of optical contrast and acoustic imaging, but does not make every molecule identifiable. Molecular and functional information depends on the absorbers or reporters available, their detectability and the ability to distinguish their signals in tissue.

The broader concept is not tied to PACT alone. Its defining advance would be the combination of useful deep-body molecular measurements and practical access. Demonstrating depth, speed, molecular contrast or portability separately would contribute toward that goal, but would not establish that the combined capability works in clinically relevant human applications.

significance.text: If achieved, accessible deep-body molecular imaging could make disease activity and treatment response observable in settings where specialized imaging is unavailable or impractical. Its potential importance comes from measuring biological processes that anatomy alone may not reveal. The reviewed PACT literature provides a concrete basis for this possibility: it describes measurements of blood oxygenation in and around tumors using endogenous hemoglobin contrast, alongside preclinical treatment-response monitoring. These examples establish a technical rationale, not a demonstrated general improvement in patient outcomes.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more frequent assessment of treatment response, earlier recognition that a therapy is ineffective and wider access to molecularly informed decisions. Those benefits would depend on the particular measurement being reliable and actionable, and on the complete service being affordable and usable. A smaller scanner alone would not establish better access if acquisition, staffing, interpretation or any required contrast agents remained impractical. These are implications of the proposed capability rather than outcomes demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

The impact should be judged application by application. A measurement of oxygenation is not equivalent to identification of arbitrary molecules, and success in selected tissues would not establish comprehensive whole-body coverage. Replacing most biopsies or all existing scanners would require separate evidence that the new measurements answer the relevant clinical questions with acceptable reliability. Neither replacement claim follows from the current proposal.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an integrated system that preserves clinically useful molecular discrimination at meaningful human-body depths while meeting the resolution, speed, safety and cost requirements of its intended applications. In PACT, optical scattering and attenuation constrain how much excitation reaches a target. The November 2024 review states that strong optical attenuation largely prevents conventional PACT from imaging targets beyond a few centimeters. Increasing depth therefore involves more than improving the detector: sufficient excitation and detectable contrast must remain available at the target.

Quantitative interpretation is a separate obstacle from detecting a structure. Optical fluence—the light available locally to excite a signal—varies with wavelength, depth and target. Consequently, a measured signal cannot automatically be interpreted as a direct measure of target abundance or biological activity. Molecular discrimination must account for this uncertainty and distinguish relevant absorbers or reporters despite limited signal and potentially similar optical responses. The supplied evidence does not define a universal target-discrimination benchmark.

Other barriers include sensitivity, limited-view artifacts, reconstruction reliability and the tradeoff between imaging speed and field of view. Capturing a rapid process over a large region is a different engineering task from collecting a detailed image of a small or stationary target. Detector configuration, illumination geometry and equipment cost also affect whether a system can move beyond specialized research environments. Improvements must work together under the same operating conditions to establish the proposed combined capability.

The review discusses deeper imaging through internal illumination or X-ray excitation, while identifying limits on their general applicability. Such approaches alter the access geometry or excitation method and must be evaluated on their own terms. Their depth achievements cannot simply be transferred to a portable system using external optical illumination, nor do they by themselves resolve the proposal's combined safety and deployment requirements.

current_state.text: Menozzi and Yao's review, published on 6 November 2024, describes extensive preclinical and emerging clinical applications of PACT. It establishes the imaging mechanism and documents progress beyond the optical diffusion limit. Its account supports PACT as a relevant platform for deep-tissue functional and molecular imaging, while leaving substantial barriers to broader clinical translation.

The reviewed demonstrations cover different scopes: whole-body small-animal imaging, whole-breast imaging, superficial high-speed imaging and deeper imaging with internal illumination. These achievements involve different subjects, targets, geometries and excitation conditions. Whole-body coverage in a small animal does not establish whole-human-body coverage; whole-breast imaging does not establish access to every deep organ; and superficial imaging speed does not establish the same speed at depth. Their strongest individual features cannot be combined into evidence for a single universal scanner.

A concrete functional capability is the use of hemoglobin contrast to measure blood oxygenation inside and around tumors, with preclinical applications to treatment-response monitoring described in the review. This illustrates useful biological information derived from a particular absorber. It does not establish unrestricted molecular identification, general clinical benefit or equivalent performance for unrelated targets. Conventional optical excitation also remains substantially constrained beyond a few centimeters, according to the review.

The supplied evidence does not establish a handheld, real-time, whole-human-body scanner that resolves arbitrary molecules. Whether all those capabilities can be combined remains uncertain; this limitation is not proof that the broader innovation is impossible. The documented account is dated to November 2024. Retrieval of the source in November 2026 does not update its scientific coverage, and the empty search record does not establish subsequent progress through the review's stated 1 November 2026 cutoff or the present task date.

The supplied review reports that the retained HTML contained the complete article text, including references and end matter, and that its identity was verified. The source index also records a verified, untruncated PDF extraction without reported extraction issues. Figure images were not inspected in the supplied evidence review, so no figure-dependent measurements are asserted here. The available assessment therefore supports the textual findings without providing an independent audit of every underlying experimental study.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently validate a portable or otherwise broadly deployable system for several clinically important deep-body targets, comparing it with appropriate reference standards and current imaging methods. The selected applications should define what counts as a target, what molecular or functional information is being measured and what clinical decision the measurement is intended to support. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independently validated deployable imaging of several clinically important deep-body targets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance boundaries: establish acceptable depth, target discrimination, spatial resolution, imaging speed, field of view, safety and deployment cost for each application before evaluating success. Report these properties together for the tested configuration, including relevant patient and tissue conditions. A convincing demonstration should show that the combined performance is achieved in the same use case, rather than assembling favorable specifications from different instruments or experiments. The supplied evidence does not justify universal numerical thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Predefined application-specific performance boundaries met in the same configuration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: independent groups should reproduce clinically relevant measurements and characterize measurement uncertainty, repeatability, failure modes and sensitivity to operating conditions. For PACT-based implementations, validation should address depth- and wavelength-dependent fluence, limited-view artifacts and the distinction between detecting a signal and accurately estimating the underlying biological quantity. These proposed checks respond to barriers documented in the review; they are not a source-defined certification procedure.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of clinically relevant measurements with quantified uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: show that using the system improves decisions or access in its intended care settings, alongside acceptable safety and a measured account of deployment costs and operational requirements. Define 'several targets' and 'broadly deployable' in advance so those claims can be assessed. Successful finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth across the tested applications and populations, not literal universality or the ability to resolve arbitrary molecules throughout every human body.
completion_criteria.label: Improved care decisions or access with measured deployment costs

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with BME-07, 'A broadly effective early-warning test for lethal cancers': deep-body molecular imaging could help localize or characterize suspicious disease, but an imaging capability does not by itself establish effective early warning. BME-07 requires evidence that the test detects relevant cancers early enough to improve outcomes. BME-15 concerns the broader ability to make useful spatial molecular measurements, including applications beyond cancer.

Conceptual comparison with BME-18, 'Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers': both seek actionable biological measurements. BME-15 emphasizes where signals arise within the body and whether they can be imaged at depth; BME-18 emphasizes sustained measurement over time. An episodic image does not establish continuous sensing, and a continuous biomarker sensor does not necessarily provide a spatial map. BME-16, 'Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants,' could overlap with implementations requiring implanted or internally positioned components, but durable tissue integration is a separate capability and is not inherent to external imaging.

Conceptual comparison with BME-10, 'Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use': molecular imaging could supply spatial and functional observations for constructing or checking such models. Those observations would not establish that a model predicts treatment response accurately. Conversely, a predictive model would not solve the physical challenge of acquiring reliable molecular measurements deep in the body.

Conceptual comparison with BME-02, 'Programmable delivery of genetic therapies to most tissues,' and BME-05, 'Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body': suitable molecular imaging could potentially help assess delivery, localization or response. Delivery, therapeutic sensing and therapeutic action remain distinct from external measurement. Detecting a reporter would also require validation before it could be treated as evidence of therapeutic activity.

Conceptual comparison with BME-01, 'Manufacturing transplantable human organs on demand,' BME-11, 'Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body,' BME-12, 'Reliable, scalable animal-to-human organ transplantation,' and BME-17, 'Minimally invasive assembly of functional tissue inside the body': imaging could potentially help assess tissue condition, perfusion or response during these interventions. Such monitoring would support their evaluation without establishing organ manufacture, regeneration, transplantation or tissue assembly. BME-15 remains a measurement capability rather than a tissue-producing or replacement intervention.

change_log.reason: The research and review support a coherent innovation spanning molecular discrimination, depth, speed, resolution, safety and access; no single unsupported assertion warrants removing it.

change_log.reason: No historical specification was supplied, and the human scope needed to be distinguished from small-animal demonstrations.

change_log.change: Separated optical absorption contrast, functional measurement and arbitrary molecular identification.
change_log.reason: PACT relies on detectable absorbers and reporters; hemoglobin-based oxygenation measurements do not establish unrestricted molecular discrimination.

change_log.change: Integrated concrete barriers involving optical fluence, attenuation, limited-view artifacts, sensitivity, field of view, speed and equipment cost.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why individual imaging achievements do not yet establish the combined proposed capability.

change_log.change: Separated small-animal, breast, superficial high-speed and internally illuminated demonstrations.
change_log.reason: Their different subjects and operating conditions prevent treating their capabilities as a single demonstrated human scanner.

change_log.reason: Completion should cover the full stated problem while keeping proposed requirements distinct from established standards.

change_log.reason: Technical feasibility and selected demonstrations do not establish broad clinical substitution or benefits across untested applications.

unresolved_issues: Progress after the November 2024 review remains unverified; the supplied material cannot establish the comprehensive state of the field in November 2026.
The target applications, required depths, acceptable resolution and speed, discrimination performance, safety boundaries and deployment costs remain unspecified.
The proposal still needs measurable definitions of 'several clinically important targets' and 'broadly deployable.'
The supplied evidence does not resolve whether useful depth, molecular discrimination, speed, coverage, safety and access can be achieved together in one practical system.
Figure images and the underlying experimental studies were not independently assessed in the supplied review, limiting experimental detail and quantitative comparisons.
Improved clinical decisions, patient outcomes, access and replacement of existing diagnostic procedures require application-specific evidence beyond the supplied technical review.

brief.title: Widely available scans of disease activity deep in the body
possible: Patients could have disease activity and treatment response measured deep inside their bodies in care settings where specialized scans are impractical. Clinicians could track selected molecules and biological processes, alongside the shapes of organs and tissues.
why: These measurements could reveal changes that anatomy alone misses. More frequent checks could help clinicians recognize sooner when a treatment is failing and make treatment decisions available to more patients.

sources.showed: Their review describes photoacoustic imaging, which uses light to generate sound inside tissue. It covers measurements of tumor blood oxygenation and treatment monitoring in animals, alongside emerging clinical uses.
sources.quote: Combining optical excitation and acoustic detection, photoacoustic imaging achieves optical contrast with acoustic resolution at depths beyond the optical diffusion limit.
sources.cited_for: Light and sound can reveal biological activity deeper in tissue than conventional optical microscopy.
sources.not_established: The reviewed systems do not combine useful measurements across deep human organs with practical cost, speed and safety.

sources.showed: A breast scanner combined photoacoustic imaging with ultrasound, which images tissue using sound. In 61 patients, blood measurements helped distinguish benign from malignant lesions better than conventional ultrasound.
sources.quote: multispectral photoacoustic imaging was used to measure blood volume and oxygen saturation within lesions.
sources.cited_for: A clinical breast study shows that biological measurements can add useful information to structural scans.
sources.not_established: A single breast study does not establish independent reproduction, performance in other deep organs or affordable deployment.

sources.showed: In 38 prostate cancer patients, a scanner combining radioactive tracer imaging with anatomical imaging supported shorter scans and tracked the tracer through the body.
sources.quote: Objective evaluation of PET/CT image quality showed no significant decrease in tumor-to-background ratio (TBR) with shorter acquisition times, despite a gradual decrease in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the spleen.
sources.cited_for: Whole-body molecular measurements and shorter scans are possible for a selected cancer target.
sources.not_established: This study does not establish affordable deployment across care settings or performance across several molecular targets.

sources.showed: In a preprint, researchers built forearm-shaped test objects with dyes that mimic blood's light absorption. They used these objects to measure errors in imaging-based estimates of blood oxygenation.
sources.quote: Finally, we demonstrated the value of the created phantoms for oximetry validation in HSI and PAT.
sources.cited_for: Tissue-like test objects provide a way to assess errors in blood oxygenation measurements.
sources.not_established: Tests in artificial forearms do not establish accurate measurements in living patients or across deep organs.

sources.who: Mengjie Shi, Feng He, Tom Vercauteren and Wenfeng Xia
sources.showed: A preprint reports software that rapidly estimates how light spreads through tissue to correct oxygenation measurements. Human oxygenation analysis included only volunteers whose signals were strong enough.
sources.quote:
GenMC accurately reconstructed optical fluence
distributions across varying tissue geometries, preserving smooth
depth-dependent attenuation and continuity across tissue bound-
aries.
sources.cited_for: Fast correction for uneven light delivery addresses a source of error in photoacoustic measurements.
sources.not_established: Agreement with simulations and plausible oxygenation values does not establish accuracy across patients, depths or targets.

shown: Sinyoung Park and colleagues combined breast structure scans with blood volume and oxygenation measurements, improving the distinction between benign and malignant lesions in a small clinical study.

Christos Sachpekidis and colleagues demonstrated whole-body tracking of a cancer-targeting radioactive tracer with shorter scans. These results establish selected capabilities; nobody has demonstrated the full combination of deep measurements and broad access.
missing: A deployable system has yet to distinguish several clinically important targets reliably at useful depths in the human body.
Depth, detail, speed, coverage, safety and cost have yet to meet application-specific requirements together in the same system.
Independent teams have yet to reproduce the combined capability and demonstrate better care decisions or access with measured operating costs.

milestones.label: Independent validation of a deployable scanner for several deep targets
milestones.explanation: Independent testing would have to validate several clinically important deep targets against reference measurements and current scans. This would establish useful breadth in a system that care settings could deploy.

milestones.label: All performance requirements met in the same configuration
milestones.explanation: Each application would have to meet predefined requirements for depth, target distinction, detail, speed, coverage, safety and cost in one configuration. This would show that the necessary capabilities work together.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction with measured uncertainty
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to reproduce clinically relevant measurements and quantify uncertainty, repeatability and failures under changing conditions. This would establish how reliably the scans measure biology.

milestones.label: Better care decisions or access with measured deployment costs
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show better decisions or access, acceptable safety and measured costs under predefined claims of breadth and deployability. This would establish practical value in the tested care settings.

uncertain: Can useful depth, reliable molecular measurements, speed, coverage, safety and affordability be achieved together?
Which targets and care settings should define success, and what performance would make each measurement useful?

page.title: Deep-tissue molecular imaging in underserved care settings
page.definition: An imaging service maps specified molecules or biological processes in living human tissue at the anatomical depth required by a clinical indication. The service has validated clinical performance and is delivered in a care setting that previously lacked it, with assessed total costs and resource requirements.

goal.need: An IAEA-led study published on 27 August 2020 estimated that at least 96 countries needed additional PET-CT services and more than 200 additional scanners for its modelled cancer indications. Externally illuminated photoacoustic imaging generally reaches only a few centimetres. Existing whole-body molecular imaging and demonstrations of selected photoacoustic measurements therefore address different parts of the access problem.

completion.title: A validated molecular-imaging service operates in a previously unserved care setting.
completion.criterion: For one named indication, molecular target or biological process, and previously unserved care setting, the same imaging service measures the target at the required anatomical depth, meets its authorised study's prespecified clinical-performance and safety endpoints, has a favourable independent assessment of clinical utility and cost-effectiveness, and delivers examinations in that setting with audited total service costs and staffing requirements. Completion applies only to that indication and setting.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body located defines this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searched IPASC roadmaps and standards work, CRUK/EORTC and ESR validation statements, FDA device pathways and SNMMI access goals; none defined a combined depth, molecular-discrimination, cost and access test. This Atlas composite uses their application-specific validation and adoption requirements. PET already supplies deep-body molecular imaging for selected indications; the additional access claim requires evidence for a named service and setting.

milestones.title: An imaging biomarker has relative error below 15%, with ESR's low-signal exception.
milestones.criterion: An image-derived biological measurement has relative error below 15% against a known tissue or phantom reference; ESR permits up to 20% below the lower limit of quantification. These are ESR's proposed generic validation limits. Dreher et al.'s preprint of 29 March 2025 tested 10 forearm phantoms at five oxygenation levels from 0% to 100%; its mean absolute errors do not establish this relative-error test. Eight PET/CT systems in Kaalep et al.'s study held fluorine-18 FDG EARL accreditation, whose calibration-bias limit was 10%; that accreditation was tracer-specific.
milestones.set_by: European Society of Radiology, 2020 validation statement, technical-validation section; these are proposed generic biomarker criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: The relative error should be below 15%

milestones.title: A human feasibility study demonstrates the molecular-imaging measurement and initial clinical safety.
milestones.criterion: An authorised human feasibility study establishes device proof of principle and initial clinical safety. Related demonstrations: on 26 November 2025, Park et al. reported photoacoustic/ultrasound imaging of 66 breast lesions in 61 patients, with vessel signals typically visible to 29 mm. On 30 January 2024, Sachpekidis et al. reported PET/CT in 38 prostate-cancer patients given 2 MBq/kg fluorine-18 PSMA-1007; 8-minute reconstructions retained 169/169 lesions seen in 10-minute reference reconstructions.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, October 2013 early-feasibility guidance; its device-development stage is distinct from marketing authorisation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Early feasibility studies allow for early clinical evaluation of devices to provide proof of principle and initial clinical safety data.

milestones.title: An imaging biomarker has a global coefficient of variation below 15%, with ESR's stated exceptions.
milestones.criterion: The global coefficient of variation, standard deviation divided by mean, is below 15%, or at most 20% below the lower limit of quantification, across repeatability and reproducibility tests; ESR prefers standard deviation near zero. Related results: five of eight zirconium-89 PET/CT systems had aligned phantom recovery after bias correction in 2018. The GenMC preprint of 23 September 2026 analysed oxygenation in 15 of 37 volunteers selected for signal strength; it supplies no multicentre coefficient-of-variation test.
milestones.set_by: European Society of Radiology, 2020 validation statement, precision assessment; these are proposed generic biomarker criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: The global CoV should be below 15%

milestones.title: A molecular-imaging study meets its prespecified primary clinical endpoint.
milestones.criterion: Meet the indication-specific protocol endpoint. FDA's Reader-02 assessment used greater specificity than ultrasound alone at 98% sensitivity: 480 patients and 15 readers yielded a 9.0-percentage-point specificity gain, 95% confidence interval 1.0–17.0, p=0.027. PET-NECK randomised 564 patients with advanced nodal head-and-neck cancer; its overall-survival non-inferiority boundary was a hazard ratio of 1.50, and the observed ratio was 0.92, 95% confidence interval 0.65–1.32. Neither threshold transfers to other indications.
milestones.set_by: The indication-specific study protocols: Reader-02 for breast masses, reproduced in FDA's assessment, and PET-NECK for advanced nodal head-and-neck cancer, registered as ISRCTN13735240.
milestones.threshold_quote: Evaluate reader specificity with IUS alone at 98% sensitivity versus Imagio (IUS+OA) at the same sensitivity.

milestones.title: A molecular-imaging device receives marketing authorisation for its stated clinical indication.
milestones.criterion: Receive the applicable marketing decision for the device and indication; required imaging agents also need a lawful clinical-use route. FDA uses PMA approval, De Novo classification or 510(k) clearance according to device class. Imagio's photoacoustic/ultrasound breast-imaging system received PMA approval on 11 January 2021. Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT received 510(k) clearance on 3 March 2021. Device authorisation does not establish quantitative validity for every biomarker or expanded service access.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, device marketing pathways; the quoted authorisation is the PET/CT-specific K210262 clearance letter.
milestones.threshold_quote: You may, therefore, market the device, subject to the general controls provisions of the Act.

milestones.title: An imaging pathway demonstrates clinical utility and an advantage in cost per quality-adjusted life year.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate clinical utility and a favourable cost-per-QALY comparison with current care; a QALY weights survival by health-related quality. In PET-NECK's 564 patients, two-year NHS secondary-care costs were £1,492 lower per patient, with 99% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000/QALY. A 2024 optoacoustic/ultrasound breast-imaging model using PIONEER-01 performance favoured supplemental imaging in 98.69% of 10,000 simulations at US$100,000/QALY. The latter is model-based economic evidence, not an observed expansion of access.
milestones.set_by: CRUK/EORTC consensus group, Imaging biomarker roadmap for cancer studies, cost-effectiveness domains 2 and 3; no universal monetary threshold is specified.
milestones.threshold_quote: unless they offer an advantage in terms of cost per quality adjusted life year (QALY) gained

results.finding: In 61 patients, multispectral photoacoustic imaging measured blood volume and oxygen saturation in 66 breast lesions.
results.detail: The hospital IRB approved the study, and the imaging demonstrated proof of principle. The supplied text does not report clinical safety outcomes.
results.quote: In a clinical study of 61 patients with 36 benign and 30 malignant lesions, multispectral photoacoustic imaging was used to measure blood volume and oxygen saturation within lesions.

results.finding: In 61 patients with 66 breast lesions, combined PAUS and BI-RADS imaging achieved 66.7% specificity.
results.detail: The study reports diagnostic performance, but the supplied text does not identify a prespecified primary clinical endpoint or establish that it was met.
results.quote: In a clinical study of 61 patients with 36 benign and 30 malignant lesions, multispectral photoacoustic imaging was used to measure blood volume and oxygen saturation within lesions. When combined with standard US BI-RADS (breast imaging reporting and data system) scores, the system achieved a sensitivity of 96.7% and specificity of 66.7%.

results.finding: PSMA PET/CT in 38 prostate cancer patients: 8-minute reconstructions retained 169/169 reference lesions.
results.detail: The retrospective analysis had ethics approval and informed consent; lesion counts were evaluable in 34 patients. It demonstrates imaging feasibility but does not report an initial clinical safety assessment.
results.quote: Compared to the reference of PET-10 images, the lesion detection rates of the PET-8, PET-6, PET-5, PET-4, and PET-2 images were 100% (169/169), 98.8% (167/169), 95.9% (162/169), 91.7% (155/169), and 85.2% (144/169), respectively.

results.finding: In 10 forearm phantoms, calibrated photoacoustic oximetry had a vessels-only mean absolute error of 27.9 percentage points.
results.detail: The study reports absolute error in oxygen saturation, not relative error against the reference, so it does not establish the milestone’s threshold.

results.finding: In a blood-mimicking phantom, 64 frames yielded an estimated 8% relative error at the 25% reference level.
results.detail: The error is calculated from rounded figure means. The figure does not establish relative error across individual measurements or the full validation range.

results.finding: In 15 volunteers, GenMC-corrected imaging estimated mean arterial oxygen saturation at 97.59%.
results.detail: The human study had ethics approval, but the source does not report an initial clinical safety assessment. The 15 participants were selected from 37 for sufficient signal strength.
results.quote:
In contrast, GenMC-based fluence
compensation yielded physiologically consistent mean values of
77.29% (venous) and 97.59% (arterial), closely matching those
obtained using MC-based correction (77.45% and 97.62%, respec-
tively).

results.finding: Photoacoustic oxygenation measurement in one four-tube phantom had 4.35% mean relative absolute error at the 80% reference level and 25 mm depth.
results.detail: The table reports a mean absolute error of 3.48 percentage points at the 80% reference level; dividing by 80 gives 4.35%. The phantom used a blood-mimicking solution, and measurements were repeated at points along the tube.

results.finding: In 1,972 patients, photoacoustic breast imaging was associated with procedure-related adverse events in 0.5%.
results.detail: All 11 procedure-related events were considered mild. FDA approved the system based on pivotal clinical studies of safety and effectiveness; its indicated use includes assessing breast-mass vascularity and blood oxygen saturation.
results.quote:
Of the 52 subjects with AEs, 10 subjects (0.5%) reported 11 events that were 
considered related (possibly, probably, likely) to the OA procedure (Table 8). All 
11 procedure-related AEs were considered mild.

results.finding: In 9 prostate-cancer patients, PSMA-targeted PET showed tumor uptake up to SUVmax 102.0, with no severe adverse events.
results.detail: The first-in-human study had institutional review board and FDA investigational new drug approval. Most imaged tumor sites were presumed; one rectal-wall lesion was confirmed by biopsy.
results.quote: First, this radiotracer is safe to administer with only three NCI CTCAE grade I adverse events observed in the nine patients in this study, all of which were thought to be unlikely to be attributed to radiotracer administration.

results.finding: Photoacoustic liver oxygenation in 2 mice had a 10% coefficient of variation across replicates breathing oxygen.
results.detail: The study assessed relative oxygenation in two mice using one system; it did not establish a global coefficient of variation across repeatability and reproducibility tests. Measurements were made with a gantry, and oxygenation was not corrected for local fluence.
results.quote:
These dynamic studies yielded COV values of 2.9 % for SO2PAI (Air) and 
3.5 % for SO2PAI (Oxygen) within same mouse and 7.6 % for SO2PAI (Air) 
and 10 % for SO2PAI (Oxygen) across replicates (n= 2).

results.finding: PET SUVmax in a six-sphere phantom across 12 scanners: post-harmonization mean reproducibility CV was 6.05%.
results.detail: Post-harmonization repeatability CV averaged 4.88% across the nine scanners requiring additional filtering. The study reports separate repeatability and reproducibility CVs, but no combined global CV. It used a phantom; clinical feasibility requires further validation.
results.quote:
The (means ± SD) pre- and post-harmonization CV
repro
of six spheres were 9.45% ± 4.69% (range, 3.83–15.3%) and 6.05% ± 3.61% (range, 2.30–10.7%), respectively.

results.finding: PET-NECK: 564 patients; PET-CT surveillance met the overall-survival noninferiority endpoint, with a hazard ratio of 0.92.
results.detail: The 95% confidence interval was 0.65–1.32, below the prespecified noninferiority boundary of 1.50; P = 0.004.
results.quote:
The hazard ratio for 
death with surveillance as compared with planned 
surgery was 0.92 (95% CI, 0.65 to 1.32); this 
outcome slightly favored the surveillance group 
and met the prespecified definition of noninfe -
riority (upper boundary of the 95% CI for the 
hazard ratio, <1.50; P = 0.004).

results.finding: Imagio Breast Imaging System: FDA PMA approval on 11 January 2021; sample size not applicable.
results.detail: Approved for evaluation of breast abnormalities in adults referred for diagnostic imaging. Optoacoustic mode assists assessment of ultrasound BI-RADS 3–5 masses using vascularity and blood oxygen saturation.
results.quote: Approval for the Imagio® Breast Imaging System.

results.finding: Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT received FDA 510(k) clearance on March 3, 2021; sample size not applicable.
results.detail: The clearance covers the stated indications for use. The record does not identify a particular radiopharmaceutical or establish its lawful clinical-use route.
results.quote:
You may, therefore, market the device, subject to the general 
controls provisions of the Act.

results.finding: Fludeoxyglucose F 18 injection for PET: initial U.S. approval in 2005; sample size not applicable.
results.detail: The FDA label establishes a clinical-use route for the imaging agent, but it does not report a marketing decision for a PET imaging device.

results.finding: Supplemental optoacoustic breast imaging was favoured in 98.69% of 10,000 simulations; patient sample size was not stated.
results.detail: The US healthcare model used PIONEER-01 diagnostic performance and a $100,000/QALY threshold. It estimates clinical and economic benefits; it does not report an observed expansion of access.
results.quote: According to probabilistic sensitivity analysis, OA/US was the better strategy in 98.69% of 10,000 iterations.

results.finding: PET-CT surveillance in 564 patients yielded an additional 0.08 QALYs per person versus planned neck dissection.
results.detail: Over at least two years, surveillance also saved £1,492 per person. Overall survival was noninferior, and fewer neck dissections were performed.
results.quote:
The per-person 
cost saving was £1,492 (approximately $2,190 in 
U.S. dollars), with an additional 0.08 QALYs per 
person.
